stimuli.text: Water flows into a tank at a rate of $$R(t)$$ gallons per minute, where $$R$$ is a continuous function of time $$t$$ in minutes. Selected values are shown.
The function $$g$$ is differentiable. Selected values of $$g$$ are shown.

Water enters a tank at a rate modeled by $$E(t) = 10 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)$$ gallons per hour and leaves the tank at a rate modeled by $$L(t) = 5\sqrt{t + 1}$$ gallons per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 8$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the tank contains 133 gallons of water.
The curves $$r = 2 + \cos\theta$$ and $$r = 1.5$$ are drawn in the polar plane for $$0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$$.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x(y - 2)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = 4$$.
Consider the curve given by $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 48$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 15$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$x = -5$$.

The function $$f$$ is defined by the power series $$f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n\cdot 5^n} = \frac{x}{5} - \frac{x^2}{2\cdot 25} + \frac{x^3}{3\cdot 125} - \cdots$$ for all $$x$$ in its interval of convergence.

options.why: The derivative of a constant is 0; this keeps the constant term.
This is $$f(3)$$, the value of the function, not its derivative.
This drops the derivative of the linear term, which is its coefficient.

questions.explanation: By the power rule, $$f'(x) = -9x^{2} - 2x - 2$$. Substituting $$x = 3$$ gives $$-89$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan(4x)}{8x}$$?

options.why: This inverts the ratio of the coefficients.
Correct. Write it as $$\frac{4}{8} \cdot \frac{\tan(4x)}{4x}$$; the second factor approaches 1.
$$\frac{\tan u}{u} \to 1$$ only when the angle and the denominator match. Here they differ by a factor of $$\frac{4}{8}$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is indeterminate, not 0.

questions.explanation: Using $$\lim_{u \to 0} \frac{\tan u}{u} = 1$$ with $$u = 4x$$: $$\frac{\tan(4x)}{8x} = \frac{4}{8} \cdot \frac{\tan(4x)}{4x} \to \frac{4}{8}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 4x - 5 & x < -2 \\ -x - 3 & x \geq -2 \end{cases}$$. What is $$\lim_{x \to -2} f(x)$$?

options.why: Correct. The left-hand limit is $$-13$$ and the right-hand limit is $$-1$$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
A limit is never the average of the one-sided limits. When they differ, the limit does not exist.
This is $$f(-2)$$ and the right-hand limit only. The left-hand limit is $$-13$$.
This is the left-hand limit only. The right-hand limit is $$-1$$.

questions.explanation: From the left, $$f(x) = 4x - 5 \to -13$$. From the right, $$f(x) = -x - 3 \to -1$$. Since $$-13 \neq -1$$, $$\lim_{x \to -2} f(x)$$ does not exist.

questions.stem: Using a right Riemann sum with the four subintervals indicated by the table, what is the approximation of $$\int_0^{10} R(t)\,dt$$?

options.why: This is the left Riemann sum.
This treats every subinterval as width 2, but the subintervals have unequal widths.
Correct. Multiply each subinterval's width by the appropriate height and add.
This is the trapezoidal sum.

questions.explanation: The widths are 2, 1, 4, 3. Use the right endpoint of each subinterval, multiply by the width and add: $$64$$ gallons.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = 9$$ and $$\int_0^{7} f(x)\,dx = 4$$, what is $$\int_{3}^{7} \left(-f(x) + 2\right)dx$$?

options.why: This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$-1$$.
The integral of the constant $$2$$ over an interval of length $$4$$ is $$8$$, not $$2$$.
This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{3}^{7} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{7} f - \int_0^{3} f = -5$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$-1 \cdot (-5) + 2 \cdot 4 = 13$$.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 4\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^n$$?

options.why: The first term depends on the starting index; check the term for the first value of n.
The formula is $$\frac{a}{1 - r}$$, not $$\frac{a}{1 + r}$$.
This divides by $$r$$ instead of $$1 - r$$.
Correct. Geometric with first term $$4$$ and ratio $$\frac{1}{5}$$.

questions.explanation: $$|r| = \left|\frac{1}{5}\right| < 1$$, so the series converges to $$\frac{4}{1 - \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)} = 5$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis so that its position at time $$t \geq 0$$ is $$x(t) = t^{3} - 12t^{2} + 45t$$. What is the acceleration of the particle at $$t = 3$$?

options.why: This is the velocity $$v(3)$$, the first derivative.
This drops the constant term of the second derivative.
Correct. $$a(t) = x''(t) = 6t - 24$$.
Sign error in the constant term of the acceleration.

questions.stem: What is $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(x^2 + 2)\right)$$?

options.why: This leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
Correct. This is the chain rule: the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.
This makes a sign or coefficient error in the outer derivative.
This differentiates the inside but then substitutes it incorrectly into the outer derivative.

questions.explanation: Treat $$\ln(x^2 + 2)$$ as a composite and apply the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\ln(x^2 + 2)\right) = \frac{2x}{x^2 + 2}$$.

questions.stem: A particle has velocity $$\vec{v}(t) = \langle 2t + 3, 3t^{2} + 1 \rangle$$ and position $$(1, 4)$$ at $$t = 0$$. Where is the particle at $$t = 3$$?

options.why: Correct. Add the integral of each velocity component to the starting coordinate.
This is the displacement; add the starting position.
This is the velocity at the final time, not the position.
This adds the final velocity instead of the accumulated change in position.
This applies the power rule to the derivative of the inside instead of to the inside function.
This differentiates the outer power but leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This is the value of the function, not its derivative.

questions.stem: $$\int \left(15x^{4} - 1\cdot\frac{1}{x} + 3e^{x}\right)dx =$$

options.why: After raising the power, divide by the new exponent.
This differentiates instead of antidifferentiating.
Correct. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power; the antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|; e^x is its own antiderivative.
The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, not a power of x.

questions.explanation: Term by term: $$\int 15x^{4}dx = 3x^{5}$$, $$\int \frac{-1}{x}dx = -\ln|x|$$, and $$\int 3e^x dx = 3e^x$$. Add the constant of integration.

questions.stem: A curve is defined by $$x = t^{2} - 3t$$ and $$y = t^{3} + t$$. What is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ at $$t = -2$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{13}{-7}$$.
This is $$\frac{dy}{dt}$$ alone.
This divides second derivatives, which is not the slope.
This is $$\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}$$, upside down.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 18x^{2} + 30x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative minimum?

options.why: This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.
Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x - 1)(x - 5)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$x = 5$$.
$$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from positive to negative, which gives a relative maximum.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 36x + 30 = 6(x - 1)(x - 5)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$1$$, negative between $$1$$ and $$5$$, positive right of $$5$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$1$$ and a relative minimum at $$5$$.

questions.stem: A quantity $$y$$ satisfies $$\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$$ and doubles every 7 hours. What is the value of $$k$$?

options.why: Solving $$7k = \ln 2$$ requires dividing by $$7$$.
Doubling means e^{kT} = 2; solve with a logarithm.
This is not a solution of e^{kT} = 2.
Correct. $$y = y_0e^{kt}$$ and $$e^{7k} = 2$$.

questions.stem: A twice-differentiable function $$f$$ satisfies $$f'(-3) = 0$$ and $$f''(-3) = -5$$. Which of the following must be true?

options.text: There is not enough information to classify $$x = -3$$.
options.why: The second derivative test applies because f″ ≠ 0.
Correct. f′ = 0 and f″ < 0: the graph is concave down at a horizontal tangent.

options.text: $$f$$ has a point of inflection at $$x = -3$$.
options.why: f″ is not zero, so this is not a candidate for inflection.
A minimum needs f″ > 0.

questions.explanation: By the Second Derivative Test, $$f'(c) = 0$$ with $$f''(c) < 0$$ gives a relative maximum.

questions.stem: At what value of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f(x) = x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 2x$$ have a point of inflection?

options.why: Sign error when solving f″(x) = 0.
Correct. $$f''(x) = 6x + 6$$ is zero and changes sign at $$x = -1$$.
This is −b/(2a), the vertex formula for a parabola, applied to the cubic's coefficients. Set f″(x) = 0 instead.
Inflection points are where f″ changes sign, not where f″ has its constant term.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 3x^{2} + 6x - 2$$ and $$f''(x) = 6x + 6$$. $$f''$$ is linear, so it changes sign at its zero, $$x = -1$$.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(0) = -5$$, $$f'(0) = 4$$, $$f''(0) = -5$$ and $$f'''(0) = 2$$. What is the coefficient of $$x^3$$ in the Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 0$$?

options.why: This divides by 3 instead of $$3! = 6$$.
This forgets to divide by $$3!$$.
This is the coefficient of the squared term.

questions.explanation: The coefficient of $$x^k$$ is $$\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}$$; for $$k = 3$$ it is $$\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$$.

questions.stem: The radius of a circle is increasing at a constant rate of 3 centimeters per second. At the instant when the radius is 4 centimeters, what is the rate of change of the area?

options.why: This forgets to multiply by the given rate of change of the dimension.
This substitutes into the original formula instead of its derivative.
Correct. Differentiate $$A = \pi r^2$$ with respect to $$t$$: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}$$.
This leaves out a factor from differentiating the formula with respect to time.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}$$. Substitute the dimension $$4$$ and its rate $$3$$ to get $$24\pi$$ (cubic or square centimeters per second).

questions.stem: What is the radius of convergence of $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{n\,(x - 3)^n}{2^n}$$?

options.why: Correct. The ratio test gives $$\frac{|x - 3|}{2} < 1$$.
The series converges for all x only when the ratio limit is 0 for every x.
The radius is the reciprocal of this.
The center is not the radius.

questions.explanation: $$\left|\frac{(n + 1)(x - 3)^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{2^n}{n(x - 3)^n}\right| = \frac{n + 1}{n}\cdot\frac{|x - 3|}{2} \to \frac{|x - 3|}{2}$$. Convergence needs this below 1, so $$R = 2$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^{2} - 4 & x \leq -1 \\ -3x - 6 & x > -1 \end{cases}$$. Which of the following is true?

options.text: $$f$$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at $$x = -1$$.
options.why: The one-sided limits match, so $$f$$ is continuous.
The one-sided slopes differ, so $$f$$ is not differentiable.

options.text: $$f$$ is continuous but not differentiable at $$x = -1$$.
options.why: Correct. The left piece gives $$f(-1) = -3$$ with slope $$-2$$; the right piece approaches $$-3$$ with slope $$-3$$. The values match but the slopes do not, so the graph has a corner.

options.text: $$f$$ is differentiable but not continuous at $$x = -1$$.
options.why: Differentiability implies continuity, so this can never happen.

questions.explanation: The left piece gives $$f(-1) = -3$$ with slope $$-2$$; the right piece approaches $$-3$$ with slope $$-3$$. The values agree (continuous), but the one-sided derivatives disagree (not differentiable).

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \cos\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$$

III. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}$$

options.why: Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II diverges, III converges.
Correct. I: converges (alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges). II: diverges (terms approach 1 (nth term test)). III: converges (p-series with p = 2 > 1).
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II diverges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II diverges, III converges.

questions.explanation: Series I converges: alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges. Series II diverges: terms approach 1 (nth term test). Series III converges: p-series with p = 2 > 1.

options.why: The numerator is not the derivative of the denominator, so this is not a logarithm.

Integrating both factors separately and multiplying is not valid.

options.why: Not this one: alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges.

questions.stem: The sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^{3}}$$ is approximated by its first 4 terms. What is the smallest upper bound on the error given by the alternating series error bound?

options.why: This is the last term used, not the first one omitted.
Correct. The error is at most the first omitted term.
This skips a term: the bound is the very next term.
The exponent stays the same as in the series.

questions.explanation: The terms alternate, decrease in size and approach 0, so $$|S - S_{4}| \leq b_{5} = \frac{1}{5^{3}}$$.

questions.stem: The base of a solid is the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}$$, the x-axis, and $$x = 6$$. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are semicircles. What is the volume of the solid?

options.why: This is the volume for cross sections that are isosceles right triangles with a leg in the base.
Correct. Each cross section has diameter $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{\pi}{8}x$$; integrate from 0 to 6.
This is the volume for cross sections that are equilateral triangles.
This is the volume for cross sections that are squares.

questions.explanation: The cross section at $x$ has diameter $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{\pi}{8}x$$. Integrating from 0 to 6 gives $\frac{9\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}$$ with $$y(0) = 6$$?

options.why: At $$x = 0$$ this gives $$\sqrt{6}$$, not $$6$$: the constant must be $$6^2$$.
The initial value is positive, so the positive root is needed.
Correct. $$y\,dy = x\,dx$$ gives $$y^2 = x^2 + C$$; $$C = 36$$, and the positive root matches $$y(0) = 6$$.
This would have dy/dx = 1, which is not x/y.

questions.explanation: Separate: $$\int y\,dy = \int x\,dx$$, so $$\frac{y^2}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2} + C$$. With $$y(0) = 6$$, $$y^2 = x^2 + 36$$ and $$y = \sqrt{x^2 + 36}$$.

questions.stem: For the curve $$x = t^2$$, $$y = t^{3} - 3t$$, what is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at $$t = 2$$?

options.why: This forgets to divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt}$$.
This is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$, the first derivative.
Correct. Differentiate $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with respect to $$t$$, then divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t$$.
This divides $$y''(t)$$ by $$x''(t)$$, which is not the second derivative.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2} - \frac{3}{2t}$$. Its $$t$$-derivative is $$\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2t^2}$$, which is $$\frac{15}{8}$$ at $$t = 2$$. Dividing by $$2t = 4$$ gives $$\frac{15}{32}$$.

questions.stem: The region enclosed by $$y = 2x$$ and $$y = x^2$$ is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.why: This squares the difference of the radii instead of taking the difference of the squares.
Correct. $$\pi\int_0^{2} \left[(2x)^2 - (x^2)^2\right]dx$$: outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
This is π times the area of the region, not a volume of revolution.
This uses only the outer radius (a disc instead of a washer).

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{30}{4!}\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{4}$$.

options.why: This divides the output by the input, which is not a rate of change.

questions.explanation: The slope of the secant line through the neighboring points estimates the derivative: $$g'(4) \approx \frac{-4 - (8)}{3} = -4$$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx$$?

options.why: This is the change in the integrand, not the integral.
This integrates over only half of the interval.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx \approx 1.111$$.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$$ with $$f(1) = -2$$. Using the tangent line at $$x = 1$$, what is the approximation of $$f(1.1)$$?

options.why: Sign error in the step.
This adds the slope without multiplying by the step 0.1.

questions.explanation: At $$(1, -2)$$, $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -1$$. The tangent line gives $$f(1.1) \approx -2 + (-1)(0.1) = -2.1$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{9} \frac{1}{x + 3}\,dx$$?

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with $$x'(t) = \cos\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right)$$ and $$y'(t) = e^{t/2}$$. What is the total distance the particle travels from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 3$$?

This is the speed at the final time.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $$r = 3 + 1\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}$$ and the rays $$\theta = 0$$ and $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?

options.why: This leaves out the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$.
Correct. $$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} r^2\,d\theta$$ on the calculator.
This divides by $$\pi$$, which is not part of the formula.
The radius must be squared.

questions.explanation: $$A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \left(3 + 1\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}\right)^2 d\theta \approx 9.084$$.

questions.stem: What is the length of the curve $$y = \sin x$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$?

options.why: This squares the function instead of the derivative.
This is the straight-line distance between the endpoints, which is shorter than the curve.
Correct. $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + \left(\cos x\right)^2}\,dx$$ on the calculator.
This is only the vertical change.

questions.explanation: $$L = \int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + \left(\cos x\right)^2}\,dx \approx 1.311$$.

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 19 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{9}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 7$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 94 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 7$$?

options.why: This is only the sand added; include the initial amount.
Correct. $$94 + \int_0^{7} R(t)\,dt$$.
This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.
This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$94 + \int_0^{7} R(t)\,dt \approx 94 + 157.220 = 251.220$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{6}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = \cos(2x)$$?

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 84 + 11\sin\left(\frac{t}{6}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 8$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

parts.prompt: How many gallons of water enter the tank during the time interval $$0 \leq t \leq 8$$?

rubric.criterion: Writes a definite integral of $$E$$ over the interval.

parts.prompt: Is the amount of water in the tank increasing or decreasing at time $$t = 5$$? Give a reason for your answer.

rubric.criterion: Concludes correctly, with a reason that compares $$E$$ and $$L$$ (or uses the sign of $$E - L$$).
rubric.example: $$E(5) - L(5) \approx 1.734$$, which is positive, so the amount is increasing.

parts.prompt: At what time $$t$$, for $$0 \leq t \leq 8$$, is the amount of water in the tank greatest? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Sets $$E(t) - L(t) = 0$$ to find the critical points.
Evaluates the amount at the critical points and the endpoints (Candidates Test).
Gives the correct time with justification.

parts.prompt: How many gallons of water are in the tank at time $$t = 8$$?

rubric.criterion: Uses the initial amount plus the integral of the net rate.

parts.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed by $$r = 2 + \cos\theta$$.
Find the area of the region inside $$r = 2 + \cos\theta$$ and outside $$r = 1.5$$.

rubric.criterion: Writes outer squared minus inner squared.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{dr}{d\theta}$$ at $$\theta = 2$$. Is the curve moving toward or away from the origin at that angle? Explain.

rubric.example: Since $$r > 0$$ and $$\frac{dr}{d\theta} < 0$$, the curve is moving toward the origin.

parts.prompt: Find the slope of the line tangent to $$r = 2 + \cos\theta$$ at $$\theta = 2$$.
Find the slope of the slope-field segment at each of the points $$(-1, 3)$$, $$(0, 4)$$, $$(1, 1)$$ and $$(2, 2)$$.
Write an equation for the line tangent to the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = 1$$, and use it to approximate $$f(1.2)$$.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope at the point and writes the tangent line.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ in terms of $$x$$ and $$y$$. Is the approximation in part (b) an overestimate or an underestimate? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Uses the sign of the second derivative at the point to conclude.
rubric.example: At $$(1, 4)$$, $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 12$$, so f is concave up and the tangent line lies below the curve: an underestimate.

parts.prompt: Find the particular solution $$y = f(x)$$ with $$f(1) = 4$$.
Show that $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates implicitly, using the product rule on the $$xy$$ term.
Solves for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ to reach the given expression.

parts.prompt: Write an equation for the line tangent to the curve at the point $$(4, 4)$$.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope and writes the line.

parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of every point on the curve at which the tangent line is horizontal.

rubric.criterion: Sets the numerator equal to zero.
Substitutes into the curve and solves.

parts.prompt: Find $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at the point $$(4, 4)$$.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with the quotient rule, treating $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$.

parts.prompt: At what times does the particle change direction? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Gives both times with a sign-change justification.

parts.prompt: Is the speed of the particle increasing or decreasing at time $$t = 6$$? Give a reason.

rubric.criterion: Finds the velocity and acceleration at the time.

rubric.example: Same signs, so the speed is increasing.

parts.prompt: Find the position of the particle at time $$t = 6$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the initial position and an antiderivative of $$v$$.

parts.prompt: Find the total distance traveled by the particle from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 6$$.

rubric.criterion: Splits the motion at the turning points.

parts.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of the series. Show the work that leads to your answer.

rubric.criterion: Analyzes both endpoints with a test.
rubric.example: At $$x = 5$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$$ converges (alternating series test). At $$x = -5$$: $$-\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges (harmonic).

parts.prompt: Find the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Maclaurin series for $$f'(x)$$. Then write $$f'(x)$$ as a rational function.
Use the first two nonzero terms of the series to approximate $$f(1)$$. Show that this approximation differs from $$f(1)$$ by less than $$0.005$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the alternating series error bound with justification.
rubric.example: The series at $$x = 1$$ alternates with terms decreasing to 0, so the error is at most the third term, $$\frac{1}{3\cdot 125} = \frac{1}{375}$$.
